title: Missä: answering with -ssa and -ssä
summary: Missä asks where someone or something is. Missä sinä olet? — Olen koulussa.
objectives: Ask where someone or something is with missä.
Build an inside-location answer with -ssa or -ssä.

sections.title: Meaning and pattern
paragraphs: Singular refers to one person or one thing in these patterns.
The inessive is the in-place form, answering where.
Missä asks where someone or something is. For the inside-location pattern, put -ssa or -ssä on the taught noun stem. There is no movement into or out of the place.
keyPoints: Missä asks for a location, not a source or destination.

sections.title: Answering the question
paragraphs: Answer with the location: koulussa (“at school”) or talossa (“in the house”). A full reply includes the appropriate verb, such as Olen koulussa (“I am at school”). A short reply Koulussa gives the same requested location. The forms of olla (“be”) are provided.
A natural short reply to “Missä sinä olet?” is “Koulussa.” (“At school.”). Use the full reply when it makes the person, action or correction clearer.
A negative location statement alone does not tell the listener where you are. Give the actual location after rejecting the incorrect one; the whole negative phrase en ole is provided.
The exercises show supporting Finnish words and their meanings when recalling them is not the task. Read the complete English meaning before choosing the question or answer form.
keyPoints: Use -ssa/-ssä for this inside location; -sta/-stä means from and -Vn means into.

sections.title: Build the answer forms
paragraphs: koulussa means at school here. Koulu + -ssa gives koulussa; the back-vowel ending expresses the location.
talossa means in the house here. Talo + -ssa gives talossa; back vowel a matches talo.
kahvilassa means in the cafe here. Kahvila + -ssa gives kahvilassa.
metsässä means in the forest here. Metsä + front-vowel -ssä gives metsässä.
hallissa means in the hall here. Halli + -ssa gives hallissa; a takes the back-vowel ending.
kaupungissa means in the city here. Kaupunki changes nk to ng and adds -ssa: kaupungissa. The complete form is supplied when this stem change is not assessed.
laukussa means in the bag here. Laukku changes kk to k and adds -ssa: lauku- + -ssa gives laukussa.
kirjastossa means in the library here. Kirjasto + -ssa gives kirjastossa.
keyPoints: Use -ssa/-ssä for this inside location; -sta/-stä means from and -Vn means into.

sinä: you; subject (who or what this sentence is about). Sinä addresses one person informally.
olet: you are; verb (the action or state). Olla has the singular you-form olet: ole- + -t.
Olen: I am; verb (the action or state). Olla has the I-form olen: ole- + -n. The ending identifies the speaker.

Missä: where; question asking where someone or something is. Missä is the inessive question form: it asks for the location, not a source or destination.
kirja: book; subject (who or what this sentence is about). Kirja is the basic singular form naming a whole book.
on: is; verb (the action or state). Olla has the irregular singular third-person form on.

ole: be; main verb after the negative verb. After a present-tense negative verb, olla takes the unchanged form ole.
